newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong launches Tiananmen anniversary rallies.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong launches Tiananmen anniversary rallies.

text.p: Hong Kong's defiant democracy movement on Tuesday prepared for a series of mass rallies to condemn Beijing's bloody 1989 Tiananmen crackdown, just 28 days before China moves in to retake control of the British colony.

On the eve of the June 4 anniversary of the Tiananmen massacre, activists were busy in Hong Kong island's biggest park putting the final touches to the "Pillar of Shame", a sculpture of twisted bodies symbolising oppression.
Leung Kwok-Hung, one of the organisers of the demonstrations, told Reuters he was expecting 40,000 people to flood into the park on Wednesday for a candlelit vigil to remember those who perished.
The vigil is an annual event drawing tens of thousands of sympathisers.
A handful of demonstrators gathered late on Tuesday across the road from the Chinese mission in the territory, putting up a wreath and lighting candles.
They hung banners that said "The heroes from the people never die. Homage to the martyrs of the democracy movement" and "Turn the anger into power and end the one-part dictatorship".
"Eight years ago the first shot from the PLA was at 11 p.m. (on June 3) so we are here to commemorate those who died at Tiananmen."
Tanks of the People's Liberation Army, whose advance units have already arrived in Hong Kong, crushed the 1989 student-led pro-democracy campaign with heavy loss of life.

Activists have locked horns with civic authorities over the "Pillar of Shame" sculpture by Danish artist Jans Galschiot, accusing local leaders of censorship for refusing to let them display the eight-metre (27 ft) statue in Hong Kong parks after the rallies end.
"Our application on the setting up of the Pillar of Shame in our parks was rejected ... for political reasons," said a rally organiser Mak Hoi-wah.

In 1989, a million people flooded Hong Kong's streets in horror over Beijing's brutality, which sparked an exodus of up to half a million citizens to safer havens before more than 150 years of British rule drew to a close.

China has pledged that when it takes back Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, the metropolis of 6.4 million mostly Chinese people will become a virtually autonomous part of the motherland and will be allowed to keep its capitalist system and freedoms for a further 50 years.
Last Sunday, 3,500 people marched to China's mission in Hong Kong to demand a reversal of the "counter-revolutionary" verdict on Tiananmen, and the release of all political prisoners.

On Monday, Hong Kong future leader Tung Chee-hwa said it was time to forget Tiananmen and he criticised the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements in China, the main organiser of pro-democracy protests, branded as subversive by Beijing.
"As a member of the Chinese nation it's now time for everyone to put aside the baggage of June 4."

Tung promised in an interview with the British Broadcasting Corporation there would be no crackdown on dissidents but Hong Kong antennae are twiching at signs of strain in his administration-in-waiting.

In two outbursts in as many weeks, Hong Kong's popular and influential civil service chief Anson Chan has called for prompt elections, a credible legislature and due regard for civil liberties, and said she was prepared to quit if asked to accept policies that clashed with her principles.

Chan's agreement to stay on in her post and serve as Tung's deputy -- she is currently deputy to colonial governor Chris Patten -- was regarded with relief in Hong Kong as a sign of stability and minimal change.
"She is playing here her only trump card and I'm surprised she's had to play it this early," David Newman, political science professor at Lingnan College, told Reuters.

Plans by China and Tung to remove the elected legislature, install an appointed body instead and reduce recent political liberties have sparked anxious objections from Hong Kong's democratic movement.
Democrats in the territory fear the freedoms which underpin Hong Kong's success will be snuffed out.
On July 1 not one member of Hong Kong's new establishment will have been elected by the people, but opinion polls show Hong Kong people to be generally unfazed.
With foreign passports in hand, thousands of Hong Kong people are returning to their home, drawn by an economic boom sweeping the British colony ahead of the handover.
Opinion polls show the healthy business climate has buoyed confidence locally and accounts for the generally positive outlook many people express towards the transition.

But academics and political analysts have warned that any signs of economic fragility may sap some of that optimism and view a mixed response to a government land auction on Tuesday, often tapped as a barometer of commercial confidence, with guarded concern.
A less-than-expected price for the first lot auctioned on Tuesday unnerved investors and pared 230.73 points from the blue chip Hang Seng stock index.

The second site generated a higher-than-expected price, signalling that there was plenty of life yet in Hong Kong's sky-high property market. But it came too late to buoy the market which had closed 1.54 percent lower at 14,760 points.
Tung's actions have taken a toll on his personal popularity but have not seriously dented overall public optimism that things will only improve in the years ahead.

An opinion poll by Hong Kong University on Monday indicated 75 percent think Hong Kong people should push for democracy in China, and 55.8 percent expect human rights would improve in China within three years.
